report.source_text: Upon presentation to our dermatology clinic, physical examination revealed a 20×13 cm erythematous, hardened plaque covering most of the patient’s anterior chest wall (Figure 1). In addition, multiple ulcerations were found on the medial and lateral aspects of both ankles (Figure 2A, 2B). The lesions on her extremities presented as erythematous, friable, bleeding ulcers with a well-defined border.

report.source_text: After a dermatological evaluation, standardized wound care and oral prednisone treatment were initiated for PG. This included gentle wound cleansing with hydrogen peroxide soaks and wrapping of the lesions with mupirocin and DuoDERM twice weekly. This resulted in 50% improvement based on decreased lesion size, depth, and erythema. The patient received prednisone when she presented to our clinic. The possibility of intravenous immunoglobulin treatment was discussed with the patient for her PG. Radiation therapy for her metastatic lobular carcinoma was also discussed. Unfortunately, due to the coronavirus pandemic, no additional treatment was initiated at that time, and the patient died soon after.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Recurrent cutaneous metastatic lobular carcinoma of the anterior chest wall with concurrent pyoderma gangrenosum of the lower extremities
clinician.trajectory_summary: An 84-year-old woman with a history of lobular breast carcinoma (status post left mastectomy) and ulcerative colitis presented to dermatology clinic with a 6-year history of a slowly progressive anterior chest wall rash and bilateral lower extremity ulcerations. Physical examination revealed a 20×13 cm erythematous, hardened plaque on the anterior chest wall and multiple erythematous, friable, bleeding ulcers with well-defined borders on the medial and lateral aspects of both ankles. Biopsy of the chest wall lesion demonstrated histopathological features consistent with recurrent cutaneous metastatic lobular carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion, showing positive polyclonal keratin staining and negative E-cadherin staining. Biopsy of the lower extremity ulcers showed reactive epidermal changes and undermining of the adjacent epidermis, which when clinically correlated were consistent with well-developed pyoderma gangrenosum. Following diagnosis, treatment was initiated with standardized wound care (hydrogen peroxide soaks, mupirocin, DuoDERM) and oral prednisone for the pyoderma gangrenosum, resulting in 50% improvement based on decreased lesion size, depth, and erythema. Radiation therapy was discussed for the metastatic carcinoma. Unfortunately, due to the coronavirus pandemic, no additional treatment was initiated, and the patient died soon after.
